conflicts.fact: Reason a lone pawpaw/avocado fails to set fruit, and whether maize/Hibiscus show protandry or separate sexes
conflicts.versions: Lesson 2 says unisexual flowers (such as maize's separate tassel and silk) cannot make fruit alone and that Hibiscus is bisexual. Lesson 3 treats Hibiscus as protandrous, with anthers shedding pollen before the stigma is receptive. Lesson 7 lists herkogamy and protandry in Hibiscus. Lesson 4 says no fertilisation occurs without compatible pollen from a partner tree. Lesson 3 also lists self-incompatibility, dioecy and timing for the lone tree, while Lesson 2 attributes it only to unisexual flowers or missing partner parts.

conflicts.fact: Number and list of adaptations preventing self-pollination
conflicts.versions: Lesson 3 says there are five adaptations (protandry, protogyny, heterostyly, dioecy, self-incompatibility) but lists only four diagrams in the model. Lesson 7 uses a different set: dioecy, protandry, herkogamy, self-incompatibility, and omits heterostyly and protogyny.

conflicts.fact: Which lessons supplied which evidence (lesson numbering)
conflicts.versions: Lesson 8 says vegetative propagation is Lessons 1-2, flower features and classification are Lessons 3-5, and the double fertilisation animation is Lesson 6. In the sequence, vegetative propagation is Lesson 1, flowers are Lesson 2, self-pollination barriers are Lesson 3, double fertilisation is Lesson 4, fruit placentation is Lesson 5, and the sexual versus asexual debate is Lesson 6.

Lesson 2 says passion flower has a stalked ovary and introduces placentation using Hibiscus. Lesson 5 puts passion fruit and cucumber in parietal placentation and the bean pod in marginal placentation. Lesson 7 says tomato is a berry with axile placentation but also asks learners to dissect a tomato or passion fruit flower (not a fruit) to see ovules and placentation.

conflicts.fact: Whether passion fruit is seed-grown/variable and whether a lone passion fruit fails
conflicts.versions: Lesson 6 lists passion fruit among seed-grown, variable crops. Lesson 3 says passion fruit is self-incompatible and its farmers hand-pollinate. Lesson 7 groups passion fruit with self-incompatibility barriers. This is consistent, but Lesson 7 describes Hibiscus as having herkogamy while Lesson 2 describes Hibiscus as bisexual with no barrier.
